title: What to Eat in the Dooars: Boroli, Shidol and Momos
meta_description: A guide to Dooars food: boroli fish in mustard, Rajbanshi shidol and pelka, Bengali thalis, Nepali momos, garden-line cooking, haat markets and fair prices.
summary: Dooars food is river fish, rice and greens, cooked three or four ways. Rajbanshi homes make shidol and pelka, Bengali dhabas serve boroli fish in mustard, Nepali kitchens in the hill villages make momos and gundruk, and tea garden families keep Chota Nagpur traditions. A good thali costs ₹150–300; homestay meals are the best food you will eat.

sections.heading: A kitchen of four peoples
paras: The Dooars have no single cuisine, and that is the pleasure of eating here. The plains belong to Rajbanshi farmers, whose cooking leans on rice, river fish, leafy greens and fermented fish. Bengali families from the south brought fish curries in mustard, posto and sweets. Nepali families in Samsing, Jhalong, Bindu and the garden hills cook momos, thukpa and fermented greens. And the tea garden communities descended from Chota Nagpur families cook simple rice-and-greens meals and brew rice beer for festivals.

In practice, a homestay in Lataguri might serve you dal, rice, fried greens and a mustard fish curry; a dhaba on the highway at Chalsa will offer a Bengali thali and chow mein; a homestay in Samsing will make momos on request; and a Dukpa family in Buxa will cook rice, dal and vegetables from the slope behind the house. Eat where you sleep at least once a day. Homestay meals are usually the best food in the Dooars, and they are included in the ₹1,200–2,000 per person rate.

Siliguri, where most trips begin and end, is the place to fill the gaps. Its markets and bus stand lanes have Bengali sweet shops selling rasgulla, sandesh and mishti doi, Marwari snack counters, Tibetan and Nepali momo kitchens and cheap rice hotels serving fish and veg thalis to traders. A night there before an early train east is a good chance to eat a proper Bengali meal for ₹150–250.

sections.heading: River fish: boroli and friends
paras: The Teesta, Torsa, Jaldhaka and their tributaries supply the fish that matters most here. The prize is boroli, a small, silvery river fish that north Bengal people speak of with real affection. It is at its best in winter, when the rivers run low and clear. Cooks fry it whole until crisp, or make a light jhol, a thin curry with mustard paste, green chilli and turmeric, eaten with rice. Ask for it by name at dhabas around Lataguri, Malbazar and Jalpaiguri, and expect to pay more than for farmed fish.

Other dishes you will meet are rohu and katla curries in mustard or tomato gravy, small fish fried with onion, and tangra in a thin, peppery gravy. In the haats, the weekly village markets, look for shutki, sun-dried fish, sold in heaps and smelled from twenty metres away. River fish catches change with the season and the floods, and boroli is not always available; ask what came in that morning.

sections.heading: Rajbanshi dishes: shidol and pelka
paras: Rajbanshi cooking is the oldest kitchen of the Dooars plains and the least seen by visitors, because it lives in homes rather than restaurants. Two dishes are worth asking for.

Shidol is a fermented fish preparation: small fish, typically puti, dried and pounded with the stems of arum or similar plants, shaped into cakes and kept in earthen pots to ferment. A little shidol is roasted or fried and mashed with garlic, chilli and onion into a pungent chutney eaten with rice. It is strong, salty and an acquired taste. Pelka is a dish of leafy greens, often jute leaves, cooked with chheka, an alkaline water traditionally made by filtering through ash, which softens the leaves and gives a slightly slippery, soupy texture.

Few dhabas cook these. Ask your homestay host if a Rajbanshi family nearby could make them, or look for food stalls at fairs such as the Jalpesh mela near Maynaguri around Shivaratri. Be patient with the strength of shidol; locals start children on a very small amount.

sections.heading: Hill kitchens and garden lines
paras: Up the side valleys, at Samsing, Suntalekhola, Jhalong and Bindu, the food turns Nepali. Momos come steamed or fried with chicken, pork or vegetables and a fierce tomato and chilli achar. Thukpa, a noodle soup, is the cheap supper of cool evenings. Ask homestay hosts for gundruk, fermented and dried leafy greens cooked into a sour soup, and kinema, fermented soybeans fried with onion and chilli. Sel roti, a ring of sweet rice-flour batter fried in oil, appears at festivals and on cold mornings with tea.

In the tea garden areas, families descended from Oraon, Munda and other Chota Nagpur peoples cook rice with dal, seasonal greens gathered from the garden edges and field margins, and occasionally pork or chicken for celebrations. Handia, a home-brewed rice beer, is made for festivals such as Karam in Bhadra. It is a household and community drink, not something to buy in a bottle; if you are offered a cup at a festival, it is a gesture of welcome.
Near the Bhutan border, especially in Jaigaon opposite Phuentsholing, small restaurants serve Bhutanese food: ema datshi, chillies cooked in cheese, red rice and buckwheat noodles.

sections.heading: Eating well without overspending
paras: Food is one of the easier places to save money in the Dooars, and the cheap choices are usually the tastier ones.
list: Choose a homestay with meals included rather than a room-only resort; you will eat better and spend half as much.
Eat lunch at the busiest dhaba on the highway, where the fish is fresh because it sells out by 2 pm.
On safari days, ask your host for a packed breakfast of puri, eggs or bread before the 6 am slot, and eat properly afterwards.
Order fish by the piece; dhabas price boroli and large fish per plate or per piece, so ask before you order.
Carry water and biscuits on long transfers; forest stretches between Chalsa and Nagrakata, and around Buxa and Jayanti, have few shops.
Buy fruit at haats and bazaars rather than at tourist stalls near the park gates, where prices are higher.

sections.heading: Tea, fruit and the weekly haat
paras: The Dooars grow tea by the tonne, almost all of it CTC, the crush, tear and curl method that makes the strong, quick-brewing leaf behind India's milky chai. A stall glass costs ₹10–20, boiled with milk and sugar. Some garden shops sell packets of local CTC; carry a few home for the taste of the plains.

Areca palms stand around nearly every village house, and betel nut with paan leaf is chewed everywhere. Pineapples come from the farms around Bidhannagar near Siliguri in summer; jackfruit and lychees ripen in May and June. In winter, look for oranges brought down from the hills, and fresh greens of every kind.

The best place to see all this is a haat, the weekly market held on a fixed day in each area. Rajbanshi farmers bring vegetables and fish, garden families buy rice and cloth, traders from the hills sell oranges and ginger, and the tea stalls run all day. Ask your host which day the nearest haat falls on. Go in the morning, carry small notes, and ask before you photograph sellers.

faqs.a: Boroli is a small, silvery river fish from the Teesta, Torsa and other north Bengal rivers, prized in the Dooars and Jalpaiguri. It is best in winter, fried whole until crisp or cooked in a light mustard and green chilli jhol with rice. Ask for it at dhabas around Lataguri and Malbazar; availability depends on the catch.

Shidol is a Rajbanshi fermented fish preparation. Small fish are dried, pounded with plant stems such as arum, shaped into cakes and fermented in earthen pots. A little is roasted and mashed with garlic, chilli and onion into a pungent chutney eaten with rice. It is rarely on dhaba menus, so ask a homestay host.

faqs.q: Is vegetarian food easy to find in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Yes. Every dhaba serves a veg thali of rice, dal, a vegetable dish, fried greens and papad for ₹100–180, and homestays cook vegetarian meals on request. Momos come with vegetable fillings in the hill villages. Tell your host in advance, as fish is the default in many homes.

faqs.q: What food should we try in Lataguri?
faqs.a: A fish thali at a highway dhaba, boroli fry or jhol in winter if it is available, and dinner at your homestay, where hosts often cook mustard fish curry, dal, fried greens and rice. Ask if a Rajbanshi neighbour could make shidol chutney or pelka. Expect ₹150–300 for a fish thali.

faqs.q: Are homestay meals good in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Usually they are the best food of the trip: home-cooked rice, dal, seasonal greens, fish or chicken curry and pickles, included in the ₹1,200–2,000 per person rate with dinner and breakfast. Tell hosts about dietary needs and spice levels early, since they shop for meals in the morning.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat street food in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Generally, if you choose busy stalls where food is cooked fresh and hot in front of you. Momos, thukpa, chow mein and pakoras are safe bets. Avoid cut fruit sitting in the sun and drink bottled or filtered water. Carry oral rehydration salts in April and May, when heat raises the risk.

Handia is a home-brewed rice beer made by Adivasi families in the tea garden areas, a tradition brought from Chota Nagpur. It is brewed for festivals such as Karam and family occasions, not sold commercially. If offered a cup at a festival, accept it or decline politely; it is a gesture of welcome.

faqs.q: Can we buy tea in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Yes. Most Dooars gardens make CTC tea for strong, milky chai, and shops in Malbazar, Birpara, Madarihat and Siliguri sell local packets at modest prices. Some garden outlets sell direct. For orthodox, whole-leaf tea, Darjeeling and Mirik shops have a wider choice.

faqs.q: Do resorts in Lataguri serve good food?
faqs.a: Some do, but most charge two to three times dhaba prices for a standard multi-cuisine menu. Unless your package includes meals, eat dinner at a homestay or a dhaba on the highway, where a fish thali costs ₹150–300. Forest corporation camps serve simple fixed menus at about ₹500–700 a day.
